ki_act-all.title: AI literacy in 15 minutes
ki_act-all.description: A short primer before you practise the 40 AI Act questions.

ki_act-l1-s1.title: Art. 4 AI Act: AI literacy is a provider and deployer duty
ki_act-l1-s1.body: The AI Act obliges providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures, to their best extent, to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. This duty is scaled: what counts as "sufficient" depends on the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of the people involved, as well as the context the AI system is meant to be used in and the persons or groups it will be used on or with. There is no single training programme that fits every role equally — a developer configuring a high-risk system needs a different level of competence than someone who merely reads a chatbot's output. This lesson covers the basic vocabulary you need to make sense of the questions that follow; for exact deadlines and the fine detail of how this duty is worded, check the regulation's own text if you're unsure.

ki_act-l1-s2.title: Four risk tiers, one mnemonic
ki_act-l1-s2.body: Prohibited – high-risk – transparency duty – minimal. The AI Act sorts AI systems roughly into these four tiers, and the tier determines which obligations apply. Prohibited practices (for example certain forms of social scoring or manipulative techniques) are simply banned outright. High-risk systems face the strictest requirements, from risk management to human oversight. Systems subject to a transparency duty (such as chatbots or deepfake generators) must disclose that users are interacting with AI. Everything else — minimal-risk applications — carries no additional obligations under the regulation, though voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged. This four-tier split is the thread running through most of the other question topics: if you can't immediately place a question, start by asking which of the four tiers the system in front of you would fall into.

ki_act-derived-verbotene_praktiken-s1.body:
A company is considering an AI system that rates employees based on their social behaviour and personal traits, producing a general 'trust score' used across quite different contexts (e.g. performance review, access to resources). How is this classified under the AI Act?

Correct answer: Such cross-context 'social scoring' of people counts as a practice prohibited under Article 5 and may not be deployed anywhere in the EU

Social scoring - evaluating or classifying natural persons over time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics, leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts - is one of the classic 'red lines' of Article 5 of the AI Act and is banned across the whole EU, regardless of individual consent.

ki_act-derived-verbotene_praktiken-s2.body:
Using 'real-time' remote biometric identification via AI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is, in principle, prohibited under Article 5. Is this true without any exception?

Correct answer: No, there are narrowly defined exceptions (e.g. targeted search for missing persons, averting a specific terrorist threat) that are subject to strict conditions and usually require prior judicial authorisation

The regulation provides narrow, exhaustively listed exceptions for real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes (e.g. searching for a missing child, averting a specific and present terrorist threat), which generally require prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation. For private companies outside law enforcement, such use generally remains prohibited regardless.

ki_act-derived-verbotene_praktiken-s3.body:
A marketing team wants to deploy an AI system that deliberately uses subliminal techniques, imperceptible to users, to manipulate their purchasing decisions and cause them significant harm. How should this be assessed?

Correct answer: This falls under the manipulative or deceptive practices prohibited by Article 5, since subliminal techniques are deliberately used to materially distort behaviour with potential for harm

Article 5 of the AI Act bans AI systems that use subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques beyond a person's conscious awareness to materially distort their behaviour in a way likely to cause significant harm - regardless of whether the target group is children or adults. A note in the terms and conditions does not change this, since the technique specifically targets unconscious influence.

ki_act-derived-verbotene_praktiken-s4.body:
An AI system is deliberately designed to exploit the vulnerability of elderly people or people in difficult economic circumstances, in order to influence their behaviour to their detriment. How does the AI Act classify this?

Correct answer: As one of the practices prohibited under Article 5, since it deliberately exploits vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or social/economic situation in order to act to the detriment of those affected

Deliberately exploiting the vulnerability of specific groups of people - for example due to age, disability, or a difficult social or economic situation - with the aim of influencing their behaviour to their detriment is one of the practices explicitly banned under Article 5. A conformity assessment or a transparency notice cannot 'cure' such a ban, because prohibited practices cannot be legalised through additional requirements.

ki_act-derived-transparenzpflichten-s1.body:
Your company uses a chatbot to automatically answer customer queries. What does Article 50 of the AI Act generally require in this case?

Correct answer: Customers must be clearly and timely informed that they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human - unless this is obvious anyway from the circumstances

Article 50 requires systems intended for direct interaction with natural persons to inform users that they are interacting with an AI system - unless this is obvious to a reasonably informed, observant person (e.g. clearly automated standard FAQ bots). A high-risk conformity assessment is not required here, since a simple chatbot is generally not a high-risk system.

ki_act-derived-transparenzpflichten-s2.body:
A colleague uses an AI image generator to create a realistic-looking video in which a well-known person appears to say things they never actually said ('deepfake'), and wants to distribute it internally and externally. What generally applies here?

Correct answer: The video must be labelled as AI-generated or manipulated, so viewers can recognise that the content and statements are not authentic

Article 50 of the AI Act requires AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that falsely appears to depict real people, objects, places, or events ('deepfakes') to be labelled as artificially generated or manipulated. Deepfakes are not banned outright, but they must be made transparent - unlike social scoring, they are not a 'red line' under Article 5, but are instead subject to a labelling obligation.

ki_act-derived-transparenzpflichten-s3.body:
An emotion-recognition AI system is used in the workplace to gauge employees' mood during meetings. What does Article 50 require at a minimum here?

Correct answer: The people affected must be informed that an emotion-recognition system is being used

For emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems, Article 50 provides for an information duty towards the natural persons exposed to the system - they must be informed that the system is being operated. This does not replace any additional labour-law co-determination rights, such as those of a works council, but applies in addition to them.

ki_act-derived-transparenzpflichten-s4.body:
From when do the general transparency obligations under Article 50 (e.g. chatbot disclosure, deepfake labelling) become applicable?

Correct answer: From 2 August 2026, together with most of the regulation's remaining obligations

Unlike the AI-literacy obligation (Article 4) and the prohibited practices (Article 5), which have already applied since 2 February 2025, the Article 50 transparency obligations only take effect on the general application date of 2 August 2026 - together with most of the regulation's remaining obligations. Companies should keep these different deadlines in mind.

ki_act-derived-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-s1.body:
A colleague wants to paste confidential customer data into a publicly available AI chatbot to get help drafting a reply. What should they consider first?

Correct answer: Personal or confidential data generally must not be entered into external AI tools without checking first, since this can violate data-protection rules and internal policy - the GDPR applies here in addition to, and independently of, the AI Act

The AI Act primarily addresses risks arising from the AI system itself, but it does not replace the GDPR. Entering personal or confidential data into an external AI tool can violate data-protection law and internal policy independently of the AI Act, for instance because the data is processed on servers outside the company's control. Both legal frameworks - the AI Act and the GDPR - must be observed in parallel.

ki_act-derived-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-s2.body:
A high-risk AI system supports the pre-selection of job applications. An employee accepts every AI suggestion without review, reasoning that 'the AI is usually right anyway'. How should this behaviour be assessed against the human-oversight requirements?

Correct answer: Problematic: human oversight for high-risk systems means critically reviewing and being able to justify the AI's suggestions, not rubber-stamping them automatically

The AI Act requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems: the responsible person must be able to understand, critically question, and, where necessary, correct or override the AI's output (avoiding 'automation bias'). Blindly accepting AI suggestions contradicts this principle and can result in discriminatory decisions, for which the company remains responsible.

ki_act-derived-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-s3.body:
A manager makes an adverse HR decision based on an AI recommendation, which later turns out to be flawed and discriminatory. The manager argues: 'The AI suggested it, I just went along with it.' Is this argument legally sound?

Correct answer: No - responsibility for a decision generally remains with the human, or with the company as the deployer using the AI system; 'the AI said so' does not remove the duty of care

The AI Act imposes obligations on deployers of high-risk AI systems, including exercising appropriate human oversight and using the system in line with the provider's instructions. These duties - and the resulting responsibility for concrete decisions made in the business - generally remain with the company or the acting individual, even where an AI provided the underlying recommendation.

ki_act-derived-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-s4.body:
A company wants to introduce a high-risk AI system for evaluating employee performance. What does Art. 26(7) of the AI Act require from an employer acting as deployer before the system is used at the workplace?

Correct answer: The employer must inform the workers' representatives and the affected employees that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, before it is put into service or used

Art. 26(7) of the AI Act obliges employers who, as deployers, use a high-risk AI system at the workplace to inform the workers' representatives and the affected employees in advance - not only afterwards, regardless of company size, and not merely in a general privacy notice.
